title: Skolem problem
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that halts on every input \(k\ge 1, c_{0},\ldots ,c_{k- 1}\in Z\) and \(u_{0},\ldots ,u_{k- 1}\in Z\), and correctly decides whether the sequence defined by \(u_{t+k}=\sum _{j=0}^{k- 1}c_{j} u_{t+j}\) for all \(t\ge 0\) has \(u_{t}=0\) for some integer \(t\ge 0\)?
definitions: All integers, including k, are given in binary with signs and delimiters; the input explicitly lists exactly k coefficients and k initial values. These data uniquely define the infinite integer sequence. The order k is unrestricted and is part of the input, not a fixed parameter. Coefficients may vanish, the supplied recurrence need not be of minimal order, and no simplicity, non-degeneracy or nonzero-leading-product promise is imposed. The search includes the given initial terms and all subsequent nonnegative indices. There is no supplied upper bound on t. The required output is YES exactly when a zero occurs and NO otherwise; only termination and correctness are demanded, without a time or space bound. This is the discrete recurrence problem over integers, not the continuous-time Skolem problem or the question whether every term is nonnegative.

context_blocks.text: A short recurrence determines infinitely many exact integer values. Testing any particular term is effective, but deciding that no term will ever be zero requires a terminating procedure for a global property. Even this elementary linear evolution leaves an unresolved boundary between arithmetic structure and algorithmic decision.

The Skolem–Mahler–Lech theorem constrains zero sets to a finite union of arithmetic progressions together with a finite exceptional set. That qualitative description is not, by itself, an algorithm that determines all exceptional zeros from the input. The distinction explains why a structural theorem about the sequence does not automatically settle the decision question.

Bilu and coauthors study simple recurrences and relate termination of their proposed procedure to transcendence conjectures. The arbitrary integer recurrence in this card also allows repeated characteristic roots and other cases outside the simple setting. Conditional termination for a subclass therefore has a different scope from an unconditional decision algorithm for the full input domain.

Bacik, Ouaknine and Worrell improve the complexity of low-order and bounded-index versions. Their July 2026 revision places the unrestricted order-at-most-four problem in coRP. A bounded index range is additional input, and an order bound of four excludes general recurrences; neither restriction answers the unrestricted decision problem.

Luca, Ouaknine and Worrell’s July 2026 paper obtains general decidability conditionally on a strengthened Cramér-type conjecture. Its unconditional density results for possible large zeros do not guarantee a decision for each individual recurrence. The new review preserves TCS-5773 and its original 2022 source rather than creating a second general Skolem entry.

why: Locate the decidability boundary for exact zero reachability in discrete linear dynamics.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with the stated model, domains, promises and quantifiers. A conditional theorem settles only its conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof matching the full target.

importance.reason: A longstanding central decidability problem with an elementary finite input, substantial arithmetic content, and direct links to verification and automata. The 2026 work confirms current specialist attention; the importance is independent of the record’s previous incomplete wording.

sentences: The Skolem problem asks whether an integer linear recurrence ever has a zero term.
Its order, coefficients and initial values form a finite binary input, with no restriction to simple or non-degenerate sequences.
The classical structural theorem about zero sets does not provide an unconditional decision procedure for every recurrence.
The reviewed July 2026 results establish stronger low-order bounds and a general conditional decidability theorem, leaving the unrestricted unconditional target unresolved.
The completed card preserves the original identifier and source while spelling out the exact discrete recurrence model.
